All four silver halides can be made by the direct reaction of their elements. Silver bromide is soft, pale yellow and unusually light-sensitive — it became the basis of modern photographic film.

Blended with silicon dioxide as 'silica-germania,' germanium dioxide raises glass's refractive index without raising its viscosity — precisely the control a fiber-optic cable's light-guiding core needs.

Bismuth and tellurium powders sealed together under vacuum and heated to 800 °C fuse into bismuth telluride, the working crystal inside every solid-state Peltier cooler and portable thermoelectric generator.
Vanadium alloyed into iron gives ferrovanadium, the additive steelmakers use as a universal hardener and strengthener — it toughens steel and makes it markedly more resistant to heat and torsion.
A nickel oxide-hydroxide plate and a metallic cadmium plate, separated in an alkaline electrolyte, make a nickel-cadmium cell — a rechargeable battery that predates lithium-ion by decades.

Platinum gauze alloyed with 10% rhodium is the catalyst ammonia burns across at 900 °C in the Ostwald process, the step that turns fixed nitrogen into nitric oxide — rhodium is what keeps the gauze from wearing through.
Cast as Pt-10Ir, 90% platinum and 10% iridium by mass, this alloy was precise and stable enough that a single bar of it served as the world's legal definition of the kilogram for over a century.
Osmiridium is not a compound but a natural alloy — grains of osmium and iridium already fused together, harder than either metal alone, found loose in the same river sands as platinum.

Small amounts of ruthenium measurably increase the hardness of platinum. It is why platinum jewellery, soft and scratch-prone on its own, is almost never sold pure — a trace of ruthenium is what actually holds a set stone.

Rhenium alloyed with tungsten makes a thermocouple that reads temperatures up to 2,200 °C, and the same alloy's high melting point and atomic mass let it survive as an X-ray tube target under continuous electron bombardment.
89% niobium and 10% hafnium, with 1% titanium this recipe cannot carry, is C-103 — the alloy used for the Apollo Lunar Module's descent-engine nozzle, and later for SpaceX's Merlin Vacuum engine.

Scandium dissolved through aluminium forms Al3Sc precipitates that pin dislocations in the metal, raising yield strength by 50 to 70 MPa. It has flown on the MiG-29 and shown up in baseball bats and bicycle frames.

Yttrium and aluminium, plus the oxygen this recipe cannot carry, crystallise into Y3Al5O12 — transparent and hard enough to host active laser ions. Doped with neodymium it became the first working Nd:YAG laser, in 1964.

Rubidium in excess oxygen gives the superoxide RbO2, alongside lesser oxides Rb2O, Rb6O and Rb9O2 — the same overshoot potassium and caesium show, and the reason none of that column forms a simple oxide easily.

Strontium chloride plugs the microscopic tubules in dentin that gum recession exposes, which is why it is the active ingredient in toothpaste for sensitive teeth. Burned, the same strontium salt gives fireworks their most intense red.
Radium mixed into copper-doped zinc sulfide phosphor is luminous paint — used on watch faces, compasses, gunsights and aircraft dials from 1908 until health concerns phased it out in the 1960s.

Welsbach's mixture of 99% thorium dioxide and 1% cerium dioxide, soaked into a fabric mantle, emits far more strongly in visible light than the flame heating it — which is why a gas lamp fitted with one burns so much brighter.

Fat Man's plutonium core sat inside a sphere of depleted uranium acting as a neutron-reflecting tamper. Plutonium and uranium, not steel, are what a real implosion-type weapon core is actually built from.

Alpha particles off polonium striking beryllium convert to neutrons, about 93 for every million alpha particles — the same Po-BeO reaction used in real neutron sources, and historically in weapon neutron initiators.

Cerium-rich mischmetal alloyed with iron is ferrocerium. Cerium's own ignition point is only 150 to 180 °C, so a striker shaving sparks off the alloy throws particles that flare past 3,300 °C — the true 'flint' in a modern lighter.

Neodymium and iron, with the boron this recipe cannot carry, form Nd2Fe14B — neodymium magnets, the strongest type of permanent magnet sold commercially, developed independently by GM and Sumitomo in 1984.

Samarium and cobalt make SmCo, a rare-earth magnet with a Curie temperature up to 800 °C and stable use up to 550 °C — well past where a neodymium magnet gives out, which is why aerospace and high-temperature motors still use it.

Europium activates yttrium-based phosphors, plus the oxygen this recipe cannot carry, into the red phosphor used in television screens and fluorescent lamps — half a gram to a gram of it sits inside every colour tube TV.
As little as 1% gadolinium worked into iron alloys measurably improves their workability and their resistance to high-temperature oxidation — a small addition with an outsized effect on the metal.

Some signal lights use a luminous paint made of a phosphor that absorbs the beta radiation given off by promethium-147 and re-emits it as light — the same glowing-phosphor idea as radium paint, run on a far gentler isotope.
The everyday Vietnamese dipping sauce: one part fish sauce, one part sugar, two parts water, with lime juice for the acid, and often garlic and chili worked in too.
3 F2 + Cl2 → 2 ClF3, first made in 1930 by fluorinating chlorine gas. Once formed it is ferociously reactive with almost anything else — it can set sand on fire.
Tetrafluoromethane is the product when any carbon compound, including carbon itself, is burned in an atmosphere of fluorine gas rather than oxygen.
Carbon disulfide once was manufactured by combining carbon, or coke, with sulfur at 800 to 1000 °C — a direct reaction run at industrial scale for over a century before natural gas replaced it.
Chlorine gas led into a flask of elemental sulfur reacts at usable rates at room temperature — S8 + 4 Cl2 → 4 S2Cl2 — turning the contents a golden yellow liquid.
Phosphorus trichloride is prepared industrially by the direct reaction of chlorine gas with white phosphorus: P4 + 6 Cl2 → 4 PCl3.
SF6 can be prepared from the elements through exposure of S8 to F2 — the same method its discoverers Henri Moissan and Paul Lebeau used in 1901, still valid today.

Phosphorus pentafluoride can be prepared by direct combination of phosphorus and fluorine, P4 + 10 F2 → 4 PF5 — a real route, though a fluorine-exchange method from phosphorus pentachloride remains the favored industrial one.
Nitrogen trifluoride can be prepared from the elements in the presence of an electric discharge — real chemistry, though modern production actually runs on ammonia and fluorine instead.
Phosphorus sesquisulfide is prepared by treating red phosphorus with sulfur above 450 K — and this exact compound, P4S3, is the ignitable head of a strike-anywhere match.
Aluminium chloride is manufactured at scale by the exothermic reaction of aluminium metal with chlorine gas at 650 to 750 °C: 2 Al + 3 Cl2 → 2 AlCl3.
Ignite aluminium and sulfur together and 2 Al + 3 S → Al2S3 runs so extremely exothermic that the molten product, over 1,100 °C, can melt its way straight through a steel container.
Copper at red heat, 300 to 400 °C, combines directly with chlorine gas in a very exothermic reaction, giving molten copper(II) chloride.
The alkaline earth metals all react with the halogens to form ionic halides — magnesium's own chloride among them, even though large-scale production today draws instead from brine.
Magnesium sulfide is formed directly by the reaction of sulfur, or even just hydrogen sulfide gas, with magnesium metal.
The alkaline earth metals all react with the halogens to form ionic halides, such as calcium chloride — named as the worked example on the general page itself.
2 Na + S → Na2S, a real direct reaction — though the tonnage that matters mostly goes straight into the kraft process that delignifies wood pulp for paper.

Pure potassium sulfide can be prepared by the direct reaction of potassium and sulfur, carried out in anhydrous ammonia to keep the reaction manageable — industrial production instead reduces potassium sulfate.
Tin(IV) chloride is prepared from the reaction of chlorine gas with tin at 115 °C: Sn + 2 Cl2 → SnCl4.
Most straightforwardly, lead(II) chloride is made by the direct action of chlorine gas on lead metal: Pb + Cl2 → PbCl2.
Gold(III) chloride was first prepared in 1666 by Robert Boyle, by the direct reaction of metallic gold and chlorine gas at 180 °C — still the most common method used today.
Copper(II) fluoride can be synthesized directly from copper metal and fluorine gas at elevated temperature — at 500 °C about 53% of the metal converts.

Aluminium-copper alloys consist largely of aluminium with a small percentage of copper as the main alloying element, precipitating an Al2Cu strengthening phase — the family's main use is aircraft construction.
Magnalium is a genuine two-metal alloy of aluminium and magnesium — light grades go into aircraft and cars, and a high-magnesium grade burns as the bright fuel inside fireworks.

Sodium and potassium alloyed together are normally liquid at room temperature, a property no other common metal pair shares — used since the 1960s as the coolant inside experimental fast-neutron reactors and satellite power plants.
Tin-rich solders readily dissolve silver; their real eutectic, 22% silver to 78% tin by weight, melts at 221 °C and is the genuine two-metal alloy behind modern lead-free solder.

Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. A strong aqueous solution of lithium bromide is the desiccant used to dry air inside large air-conditioning systems.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Potassium bromide can be regarded as the first medication that actually worked against epilepsy.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Rubidium fluoride is a white crystalline solid built on the same cubic lattice as ordinary table salt.

Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Rubidium chloride dissolves so readily into cells that its most common laboratory use is coaxing bacteria into absorbing foreign DNA.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Rubidium bromide crystallises in table salt's own structure, just stretched to fit two heavier atoms.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Rubidium iodide is sold in Romania as an eye drop, 8 milligrams of the salt in every millilitre.

Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Chemists then use the resulting caesium fluoride itself as a working source of the fluoride ion in organic synthesis.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Grown as an optical crystal, caesium bromide splits light inside wide-band spectrophotometers.
Alkali metals react aggressively with the halogens to form the alkali metal halides. Caesium iodide is the phosphor screen inside an X-ray image intensifier tube, turning radiation into a picture.
Under extreme conditions, krypton reacts with fluorine to form KrF2 — but only with help: an electrical discharge, a proton beam, UV light, or a hot wire cracking F2 into radicals near the solid gas.
At room temperature titanium ignores chlorine completely — but heated to 550 °C the two elements combine violently, forming titanium tetrachloride.
Cobalt reacts directly with chlorine, bromine and iodine to produce equivalent binary halides. Cobalt chloride is a common humidity indicator, blue when dry and pink the instant it absorbs water.
Anhydrous chromium(III) chloride can be prepared by chlorination of chromium metal directly, one halogen atom at a time onto the same element famous for growing a rust-proof oxide skin.
Lanthanum tarnishes quite rapidly in air, turning completely dark within hours as it burns to form lanthanum(III) oxide.
Ce + O2 → CeO2, straight from the metal. Cerium oxide then goes to work scrubbing carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides out of a catalytic converter, or polishing glass to an optical flatness.
Neodymium readily burns at about 150 °C to form neodymium(III) oxide, and the flaking oxide keeps exposing fresh metal underneath to burn further.
Europium metal reacts directly with every halogen: 2 Eu + 3 F2 → 2 EuF3, a white crystalline compound.
Europium metal reacts directly with every halogen: 2 Eu + 3 Cl2 → 2 EuCl3, a yellow crystalline compound.
Unlike most rare earths, metallic gadolinium is stable in dry air — but moist air tarnishes it, forming a loosely-adhering coat of gadolinium(III) oxide: 4 Gd + 3 O2 → 2 Gd2O3.
Hydrogen, like some of the alkali metals, reacts explosively with fluorine, forming hydrogen fluoride — a gas that becomes the highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid the instant it meets moisture.
Lithium cobalt oxide is commonly used in the positive electrodes of lithium-ion batteries, paired against the graphite negative electrode the lithium ions actually migrate into and out of.
2 Li + H2 → 2 LiH, direct from the elements — especially rapid above 600°C, though it proceeds even well below that.

U-238 catches a neutron and becomes U-239, which beta-decays in 23 minutes into neptunium-239 — the reaction McMillan and Abelson used in a Berkeley cyclotron in 1940 to find the first element past uranium.

Plutonium-239 in a reactor catches two neutrons to become plutonium-241, which beta-decays over 14.35 years into americium-241 — the only artificial element that ends up inside an ordinary household smoke detector.
Pu-239 + He-4 → Cm-242 + n — Seaborg, James and Ghiorso fired alpha particles at plutonium in a 60-inch cyclotron in 1944, then kept the discovery secret until after the war ended.
Am-241 + He-4 → Bk-243 + 2n — 35 MeV alpha particles fired at americium for six hours in the Berkeley 60-inch cyclotron, December 1949.
A microgram target of curium-242 bombarded with 35 MeV alpha particles in the Berkeley cyclotron produced californium-245 plus a free neutron, February 1950.
Th-232 + n → Th-233, which beta-decays in 22.3 minutes to protactinium-233 — the first step of the thorium fuel cycle, on the way to fissile uranium-233.
Actinium is prepared, in milligram amounts, by the neutron irradiation of radium-226 in a nuclear reactor — Ra-226 catches a neutron, becomes Ra-227, and beta-decays to Ac-227 in 42 minutes.
The reaction 100Mo(p,2n)99mTc — 22 MeV protons fired at a molybdenum-100 target in a medical cyclotron — was demonstrated in 1971 and is still used today when technetium-99m supplies run short.
Corson, MacKenzie and Segrè made the first astatine in 1940 by firing alpha particles at bismuth-209 in a Berkeley cyclotron, knocking out two neutrons to leave astatine-211 behind.
249Cf + 12C → 261Rf* → 257Rf + 4n — a Berkeley team fired carbon-12 ions at a californium-249 target in 1969 and traced the alpha decay of the result down to its known daughter nucleus.
249Cf + 15N → 260Db + 4n — a Berkeley team fired nitrogen-15 ions at californium-249 in April 1970, claiming element 105 in a priority dispute with Dubna that ran for years.
249Cf + 18O → 263mSg + 4n — Seaborg's own team fired oxygen-18 ions at californium-249 in 1974, and the element eventually took his name while he was still alive to see it.
209Bi + 54Cr → 262Bh + n — a GSI Darmstadt team fired chromium-54 nuclei at bismuth-209 in 1981, catching five atoms of bohrium-262 before they decayed away.
The GSI Darmstadt team bombarded a lead-208 target with accelerated iron-58 nuclei in 1984, catching three atoms of hassium-265 before they decayed away.
209Bi + 58Fe → 266Mt + n — the GSI Darmstadt team fired iron-58 nuclei at bismuth-209 on August 29, 1982, and detected a single atom of meitnerium.
208Pb + 62Ni → 269Ds + n — the GSI Darmstadt team fired nickel-62 nuclei at lead-208 on November 9, 1994, catching a single atom of darmstadtium-269.
209Bi + 64Ni → 272Rg + n — the GSI Darmstadt team fired nickel-64 nuclei at bismuth-209 on December 8, 1994, catching three atoms of roentgenium.
208Pb + 70Zn → 277Cn + n — the GSI Darmstadt team fired zinc-70 nuclei at lead-208 on February 9, 1996, producing a single atom of copernicium.

Be + Cl2 → BeCl2 at high temperature — a covalent halide, not an ionic salt, since beryllium is too small and polarizing to bond like the rest of the alkaline earths. It catalyzes Friedel-Crafts reactions and feeds beryllium electrolysis.

Be + Br2 → BeBr2, beryllium metal burning directly in bromine vapor at 500-700°C. Like all of beryllium's halides it bonds covalently rather than ionically — the one alkaline earth metal too small and too polarizing to build a true salt.
Be + I2 → BeI2, beryllium metal and iodine combining directly at 500-700°C. Decomposed again on a white-hot tungsten filament, the same compound deposits ultra-pure beryllium metal back out.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form halides — though beryllium's own bonds are covalent, not ionic, unlike the rest of the group. Reducing beryllium fluoride with magnesium at 1,300°C is the main route to metallic beryllium itself.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Magnesium fluoride's own crystal stays transparent from deep ultraviolet to the infrared, which is why it coats the lenses of cameras and space telescopes.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Magnesium bromide once served as a sedative and anticonvulsant; today it survives mostly as a Lewis-acid catalyst that steers the aldol reaction.

Mixing powdered magnesium metal straight into elemental iodine, kept strictly free of moisture, makes magnesium iodide directly. Chemists use it to strip methyl groups off aromatic ethers and to steer the Baylis-Hillman reaction.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides — calcium chloride is the general page's own worked example, and the fluoride version of that same reaction is fluorite, CaF2, the very mineral that gave fluorine its name.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Calcium bromide's dense brine gets pumped down oil wells as drilling fluid, and stirred into burning coal it captures mercury before it can vent up the stack.
Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Calcium iodide has served both early photography and, more recently, as an iodine supplement stirred straight into cat food.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Strontium fluoride's crystal carries radioactive strontium-90 inside a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, decaying quietly for decades to keep it powered.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Strontium bromide goes into flares for the same reason any strontium salt does: burned, it throws off strontium's own signature deep red.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Doped with europium, strontium iodide catches gamma rays and flashes light — a scintillation crystal grown a whole cylinder at a time.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Barium fluoride stays clear to infrared light and flashes when it catches a gamma photon, which is why PET scanners use crystals of it as detectors.
Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Barium chloride is the standard laboratory reagent for weighing out exactly how much sulfate a solution is hiding.
Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Marie Curie used barium bromide's own crystallization habits to fractionate radium out of the barium ore it comes mixed with.
Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Barium iodide is the least-documented of barium's four halides — even its own reference entry has no use to name for it.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Radium fluoride even crystallizes in fluorite's own cubic form — the same column of the periodic table, just heavier and radioactive.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Radium chloride was the first radium compound ever isolated pure — Marie Curie and André-Louis Debierne's own separation of radium from barium.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Pierre and Marie Curie discovered this salt in 1898; it later glowed on watch dials until the danger was understood, phased out only by the 1960s-70s.

Alkaline earth metals react with the halogens to form ionic halides. Radium iodide is a yellow, water-soluble salt — one of the rarest compounds here, and one Wikipedia devotes only a handful of sentences to.

Phage is Greek for devourer, and a bacteriophage is exactly that: a virus that infects and replicates only inside bacteria. It starts by binding a specific receptor on the bacterium's surface, then injects its genome through the wall.

A temperate phage does not always replicate right away. Its genome integrates into the host chromosome as a prophage, copied passively every time the bacterium divides — quiet for generation after generation until something disturbs it.

A virulent phage skips the wait: it copies itself inside the bacterium, then uses its own proteins to dissolve the cell wall. The cell bursts under its own pressure and scatters new phage. The event is named for what happens to the host — lysis.

A protozoan is just a single eukaryotic cell living free, with no tissue and no colony around it. Free-living protozoa are abundant wherever there's water — fresh, salt, brackish, or just a damp patch of soil.

Eimeria is a genus of apicomplexan parasites, and most species are locked to one host for life. Three of them — E. tenella, E. acervulina, E. maxima — are the ones that matter economically, and all three live nowhere but a chicken's gut.

Coccidiosis is what Eimeria causes once it's inside an intestine: its sporozoites invade the gut lining directly. The disease spreads from bird to bird through contact with infected droppings or infected tissue.
Salmonella is a genus of rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacteria, and ordinary meat carries a real chance of being contaminated with it — chicken and pork both, by the article's own account.

An egg can carry Salmonella before it is even cracked. Contamination happens as the shell exits the hen through the cloaca, picking up whatever bacteria are on the bird's own droppings on the way out.

Viroids are the strangest known infectious agents: circular RNA a few hundred bases long, with no protein coat at all — no gene for one, even. Every host they're known to infect is a plant, reached by aphids, contaminated tools, or simple leaf contact.

Salicin is metabolised in the human gut into salicylic acid, the part that actually relieves pain and fever. Willow bark has carried this compound for at least 2,400 years, long before either had a name.

Felix Hoffmann made the first pure, stable acetylsalicylic acid in 1897 by attaching an acetyl group to salicylic acid's hydroxyl group. The real reagent was acetic anhydride, vinegar's sharper cousin, not the acid itself.

Streptomyces bacteria live predominantly in soil and decaying vegetation, most species growing as spore-forming filaments rather than loose single cells. As a genus they produce over two-thirds of the clinically useful antibiotics ever found in nature.

Albert Schatz isolated streptomycin from Streptomyces griseus on 19 October 1943, in Selman Waksman's lab at Rutgers, out of a microbe found in New Jersey soil. It became the first antibiotic cure for tuberculosis.
Regimens built on a single drug lead to rapid resistance and treatment failure. That is exactly what happened once streptomycin alone met a bacterium that reproduces about as fast as it mutates.

Streptomyces itself grows surrounded by other soil organisms it has spent eons chemically fighting. Resistance genes were already common in soil microbial communities before anyone had purified an antibiotic out of one.
Insulin extraction ran at industrial scale on pig and cow pancreas for six decades. Porcine insulin differs from the human hormone by exactly one amino acid, which is most of why it worked.
Extracting insulin at that scale took roughly two tons of pig pancreas to purify eight ounces of the hormone.
Humulin, approved in 1982, was the first medicine made by inserting actual human DNA into a host cell, E. coli, turning bacteria into an insulin factory and ending the reliance on animal pancreases.
Sweet potatoes are mostly propagated by stem or root cuttings — pieces of vine planted directly, not grown from true seed.
Brassica oleracea var. botrytis — the same species as cabbage and broccoli, bred for a dense curd of undeveloped flower buds, grown as a cool-season crop that needs steady moisture.
Cucurbita pepo var. cylindrica, a vining herbaceous plant whose fruit is harvested while the seeds and rind are still soft — a young, unripe squash rather than a separate vegetable.
Solanum melongena is a nightshade, the same family as chilli and tomato, grown for the berry-like fruit that follows its own flower.
A perennial flowering plant whose young shoots — spears — are the spring vegetable. It grows from a planted crown, and the first shoots appear each spring.
A fast-growing mustard-family root crop that grows best in full sun in light, sandy loams — the loose soil is what lets the root come up straight.
Brassica rapa subsp. rapa, a root vegetable grown in temperate fields — the average time from planting to harvest runs 55 to 60 days.
A biennial allium cultivar grown the way onions are — in loose, well-drained soil — but left up to six months from planting before it's harvested.
A Brassica oleracea cultivar grown for edible buds that grow in a helix along a thick stalk, maturing over several weeks from the bottom up.
A Brassica oleracea cultivar grown for its leaves, which never form a head, and which is hardy enough to survive temperatures as low as -15°C.
A cultivated thistle whose edible portion is the flower bud, harvested before the flower comes into bloom — once the bud opens the structure turns coarse and barely edible.
Abelmoschus esculentus is a flowering plant in the mallow family, the same family as cotton, grown for its seed capsule — mucilaginous, releasing the characteristic 'goo' once cooked.
Agaricus bisporus, the most widely cultivated edible mushroom, is grown from sterilised spawn on composted horse manure rather than on wood, unlike shiitake or maitake.
An evergreen laurel-family tree; prime named varieties don't come true from seed, so they're propagated by grafting to rootstock — the same real mechanism apple already uses in this world.
An annual Brassicaceae salad green that prefers full sun and moist, fertile soil, reaching maturity within 40 to 50 days.
A herbaceous perennial that grows from a thick rhizome; what's eaten is the fleshy leaf stalk (petiole), not the leaf blade itself.
An aquatic Brassicaceae plant with hollow, floating stems that thrives directly in clear, fast-flowing streams.

Citrus x sinensis, a hybrid of pomelo and mandarin. Growers start a rootstock from seed, then graft a bud from the named variety into its bark — the same real propagation this world already uses for apple and avocado.
Citrus x paradisi, an accidental cross between sweet orange and pomelo, first found in the 17th-century Caribbean — a second citrus hybrid grown the same way orange already is.
Prunus persica, a stone fruit tree that begins producing fruit only two or three years after sprouting, and rarely lives past twenty.
A fruit of Prunus subg. Prunus, a drupe whose fleshy fruit surrounds a single hard stone — the commercially important trees are kept pruned to 5-6 metres.
Prunus armeniaca, an orange-yellow stone fruit whose single kernel is a hard-shelled seed — a different part of the plant from the sweet flesh around it.

Nectarines are the same species as peaches, differing only by a recessive allele for smooth skin — a naturally occurring variant fixed into a nameable variety by grafting, same as any other named fruit tree here.
A trailing cucurbit vine whose fruit is a pepo — a modified berry, 91% water — historically valued in arid, sandy-soil climates as a stored source of water.
Cucumis melo, a true melon with sweet, aromatic, usually orange flesh, grown on a vining plant.
The edible berry of a dioecious woody vine — each plant is strictly male or female, and a female vine needs a male one nearby to bear fruit at all.
An aggregate fruit of many small drupelets, grown on a cane that spends its first season only growing — the fruit doesn't come until the second season's growth.
An aggregate of small drupelets, distinct from raspberry because the torus stays with the fruit when picked — grown on a first-year cane that trails 3 to 6 metres, carrying large compound leaves.
A Vaccinium shrub whose berries are harvested by flooding the growing beds with 15 to 20cm of water, then driving a harvester through to knock the floating fruit off the vines.
A perennial flowering Vaccinium shrub, ranging from 10cm to 4m tall, bearing a true berry that turns from pale green through reddish-purple to blue as it ripens.
The date palm's fruit is a drupe with a single stone, naturally wind-pollinated — though oasis and commercial growers hand-pollinate instead for a reliable yield.
Diospyros kaki, a tree the shape of an apple tree, grown mostly in Chinese, Japanese and Korean orchards — its fruit ripens only after the tree has already dropped its leaves.
Psidium guajava, a small myrtle-family tree bearing a true berry — grown from seed it fruits within two years and keeps doing so for up to forty, tolerant of brief cold down to about -4°C.
A grass of the wheat tribe, grown as a grain — it withstands cold better than any other small grain, surviving snow cover that would kill winter wheat, which already exists in this world.
A pseudocereal — not a grass at all but a flowering plant related to spinach and amaranth. What's harvested is a true seed, and by hand: the plants ripen too unevenly for a machine.
Not a grass or a cereal at all — a pseudocereal related to rhubarb and knotweed, eaten like a grain purely because its starchy seed cooks the same way.
A group of small-seeded grasses grown as a grain, highly tolerant of drought and extreme weather — a crop suited to loose, arid ground.
Sorghum bicolor, a grass grown as a cereal grain, drought- and heat-tolerant enough to be a staple crop where dry conditions rule out most other grains.
An annual Fabaceae legume grown for its edible seeds — a pulse crop whose feathery-leaved plant sets small pods holding just two or three peas each.
Phaseolus vulgaris, the common bean — a single species behind most of the world's named bean varieties, from black turtle beans to kidney and pinto.
A small, shiny cultivar of the common bean — its dried seed coat carries anthocyanins, the pigment that gives it its black colour.
A common bean cultivar named for its mottled seed coat — Spanish pinto, 'painted' or 'spotted'.
A cultivar of the common bean, kidney-shaped and dark red — the variety in which the bean family's own raw-lectin toxin runs most concentrated.
A coarser wheat grind than flour, milled specifically for making couscous and durum pasta.
Semolina is sprinkled with water and rolled by hand into small pellets, sieved to keep them separate, then steamed until light and fluffy.
The inner bark of a Cinnamomum tree, pried off in long strips once loosened — it's the drying itself that curls the strips into the familiar quills.
A Myristica seed, dried gradually in the sun for up to 30 weeks — long enough that it visibly shrinks away from its own hard shell and starts to rattle.
The unopened flower bud of Syzygium aromaticum, picked at 1.5 to 2cm long, before the four petals inside it ever open.
A spice from the Zingiberaceae — the ginger family this world's ginger already belongs to — whose seed pods are triangular and spindle-shaped, holding small black seeds.
An orchid vine grown for its seed pods — since the flower can't pollinate itself, every plant grown commercially today is pollinated entirely by hand before the pod is left to mature.
Crocus sativus is sterile and blooms only in autumn — its crimson stigmas are hand-picked and dried, and it takes about 150,000 flowers to make one kilogram of the spice.
Foeniculum vulgare, a carrot-family plant related to celery — the dried seeds are used as an anise-flavoured spice, while the bulb is eaten as its own vegetable.
A crop of the mustard family, Brassicaceae — the same family cabbage belongs to in this world — grown for its harvested seed.
The dried unripe berry of Pimenta dioica, picked green and traditionally dried in the sun until brown, resembling a large smooth peppercorn.
The star-shaped fruit of an evergreen tree native to South China and Vietnam, picked just before it ripens — six to eight seed-bearing follicles arranged in a single whorl.
A Brassicaceae plant, related to horseradish and mustard but its own separate species, grown specifically for its rhizome, which is ground into a paste.
The true fruit of the cashew tree is a drupe that grows at the end of the cashew apple — a second, separate fruit on the same stalk.
A drupe whose seed is the edible part — as it ripens in the warmth, the shell shifts colour and abruptly splits open with an audible pop, a trait growers deliberately selected for.
A species of hickory, native to the southern US and northern Mexico — botanically a drupe, not a true nut, with a single stone inside a husk.
The fruit of a Corylus hazel tree — a genuine botanical nut, with a fibrous husk it falls free of about seven to eight months after pollination.
A genus of trees in the Proteaceae family, native to Australia — the source of the world's macadamia nut crop.
The pasta filata method: curd is heated and hand-kneaded until it becomes a single smooth, shiny, stretchy paste, then pulled and cut into individual balls.
'Cheddaring': after heating, the curd is kneaded with salt, cut into cubes to drain the whey, then stacked and turned — repeated mechanical working, not ageing, is what makes cheddar cheddar.
A hard, granular Italian cheese from unpasteurised cow's milk, aged a minimum of 12 months and averaging two years — considerably longer than an ordinarily aged cheese.
A Greek brined cheese made from sheep's milk, or a mixture of sheep and goat — this world's existing brined-cheese recipe already covers the process; this is the specific goat-milk variant.
Acid-set curds — this world's own curd, from milk plus vinegar or wine — drained and mixed back with cream and salt, with no ageing at all.
Fresh milk with about 60% of its water removed by heat, then canned and heat-sterilised for a shelf-stable product — unlike condensed milk, no sugar is added.
Sugar is added to milk that's already had 60% of its water evaporated off, until it reaches roughly a 9:11 ratio of sugar to evaporated milk — the sugar itself is what preserves it.
Cream cooked with egg to thicken it — the egg protein coagulates starting around 70°C and must stay under 80°C, or the custard curdles instead of setting smooth.
Modern tomato ketchup is made from tomatoes, sugar and vinegar, with seasoning added — the vinegar and sugar content is what lets it keep without spoiling.
Maple sap, boiled down over an open fire until 20 to 50 volumes of it reduce to just one volume of finished syrup.
A paste made from dry-roasted peanuts, sent through two grinders in succession — a medium grind, then a fine one — until smooth.
Whole fruit crushed and heated with sugar to about 104°C — at that point the fruit's own acid and pectin react with the sugar, and it sets on cooling.
Starch powder milled from the endosperm of the corn kernel, with the germ, fibre and gluten all washed away.
Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3 — hit with acid or heat, it releases carbon dioxide, which is exactly what makes a batter rise.

A dry leavening mixture of bicarbonate, a weak acid and a desiccant — cornstarch, named directly by the source — that reacts on its own once dampened, unlike baking soda, which needs an acid already in the recipe.
A fermented condiment invented by two Worcester pharmacists — its two headline ingredients, named directly by the source, are anchovies and malt vinegar.
A condiment made from chili peppers — many hot sauces are nothing more than chilli, salt and vinegar.
A seed butter made from sesame seeds — hulled, toasted, and ground until they release their own oil into a smooth paste.
A solution made by macerating vanilla pods in ethanol and water, pulling out several hundred flavour compounds beyond vanillin alone.
Ground, cracked or bruised mustard seeds mixed with vinegar (or water, wine, or lemon juice) into the condiment's familiar paste.
A decapod crustacean with an elongated, swimming body, distinct from the walking crabs and lobsters — most caught species live over sandy coastal seabeds.
A heavily armoured decapod crustacean whose tail is concealed folded under its body — built to run sideways and hide in rocky crevices.
A decapod crustacean with a long body and a muscular tail, living in crevices or burrows dug into the sea floor.
An anadromous fish — it hatches in a freshwater river, grows to adulthood at sea, then swims back against the current to its own birthplace to spawn.
A mackerel-family open-ocean fish, among the fastest-swimming of any pelagic species — one of only three fish able to hold a body temperature above the surrounding water.
An avocado-based dip, traditionally made by mashing peeled, ripe avocado and salt together with a mortar and pestle.
A Levantine dip made from cooked, mashed chickpeas blended with tahini — both already real elements in this world.
A Mexican sauce and dip usually built from chopped or cooked tomatoes and onion, with chili peppers and cilantro layered in from there.
Finely shredded raw cabbage dressed with mayonnaise — the most common of the dressings real recipes use, though cabbage is the only ingredient they all agree on.
Beaten eggs fried with butter or oil in a frying pan — the base of the dish, before any filling gets folded in.
A flat batter-bread, cooked on a hot flat surface like a griddle or frying pan.
A leavened batter or dough, cooked between two hot patterned plates rather than on a flat griddle — the grid pattern is what tells it apart from a pancake.
A cooked patty of ground meat placed inside a sliced bun — the definition holds whatever else gets added on top.
A cooked — grilled, steamed or boiled — sausage, served in the slit of a partially sliced bun.
A filling — meat, cheese, sauces or vegetables — placed between slices of bread; this is the plainest real version of it.
Cooked rice stir-fried in a wok or pan, usually mixed with egg alongside whatever vegetables or meat are on hand.
A small tortilla folded by hand around a filling and eaten straight away — the game's own wrap, given a real, named filling.
A tropical crop, frost-sensitive and needing a long warm season — planted across the tropics for exactly that reason, where potato's own temperate growing season would fail it.
Grated and pressed, cassava gives up its starch as a milky liquid; washed and dried, it becomes tapioca flour or pearls.

IBDV is a double-stranded RNA virus in the genus Avibirnavirus, its capsid non-enveloped and its genome split across two segments. The natural hosts of IBD are chickens and turkeys — a virus this narrowly hosted earns its own genus, not just a species name.

Gumboro disease is Avibirnavirus at work inside a young chicken: it destroys the lymphoid follicles in the bursa of Fabricius, and the circulating B-cells with them. Infection travels the oro-fecal route, and affected birds shed the virus for about two weeks.

The gamma coronavirus genus is drawn from the avian gene pool, and its members split cleanly by bird: goose coronavirus, duck coronavirus, and Gammacoronavirus galli — named for Gallus, the chicken's own genus.

Gammacoronavirus galli is infectious bronchitis virus's real name, chicken right there in the species. Inhaled, it binds sialic-acid receptors on ciliated airway cells, stopping the cilia and filling the tract with mucus before spreading to kidney or oviduct.

E. coli commonly lives in the lower intestine of warm-blooded organisms, and its cells survive only a limited time outside the body — so finding it in dung is itself the test, which is why it's used as an indicator organism for fecal contamination.

Most E. coli strains stay harmless commensals as long as they never pick up genes for virulence factors. The ones that do can reach tissue the ordinary gut strain never touches, and in poultry the resulting fecal-oral infection is called colibacillosis.

Ascaridia galli is a parasitic roundworm, and transport hosts such as earthworms are thought to play a role in its spread. Free-range birds carry a higher risk of infection than caged ones for exactly this reason — there's an earthworm to eat.

Ascaridiasis is a disease of poultry from heavy A. galli infection, particularly in chickens and turkeys. The worm lives in the small intestine, and its eggs have thick, resistant shells that persist in the environment long after they're shed.

A satellite nucleic acid is bare RNA, exactly like a viroid, except it encodes no structural proteins of its own. It is completely dependent on coinfecting a cell alongside a full helper virus, borrowing that virus's own proteins to get copied and packaged.

Cowpox virus, genus Orthopoxvirus, is closely related to Vaccinia, the strain later smallpox vaccines used. Its usual wild reservoir is woodland voles — cattle catch it only occasionally, which is exactly how Edward Jenner first found it.

On 14 May 1796, Edward Jenner scraped pus from cowpox blisters on a milkmaid's hand and scratched it into eight-year-old James Phipps' arm. Weeks later, deliberate exposure to real smallpox produced no disease — the first documented deliberate vaccination.

Memory B and T cells built after a first exposure don't need a second signal to act again — they divide faster and answer harder the next time the same threat shows up. That is exactly what a vaccine trains in advance, before any real infection happens.

Nitrating phenol with nitric acid gives 4-nitrophenol, the classical first step toward paracetamol. The game's nitrate ion stands in for the acid's reactive nitrogen, the same kind of stand-in aspirin's own recipe already uses for acetic anhydride.
4-nitrophenol is reduced to 4-aminophenol by hydrogenation over Raney nickel — the real second step of paracetamol's classical synthesis, one reaction away from the finished drug.

The classical last step acetylates 4-aminophenol with acetic anhydride. The game's acetic acid stands in for the anhydride — the same honest substitution aspirin's own recipe already makes, not a claim that vinegar makes paracetamol.

Histidine decarboxylase strips one carboxyl group from the amino acid histidine in a single reaction, producing histamine directly. Turning that one amino acid into histamine is the enzyme's only known job.

Arachidonic acid sits pre-built into membrane phospholipids until phospholipase A2 hydrolyses it free. That release is the real first step behind every prostaglandin, and the step every NSAID ultimately works upstream of.

Cyclooxygenase converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2, the precursor every other prostaglandin is built from — the actual signal behind pain, fever, inflammation and swelling, not the injury itself.
2 Be + O2 → 2 BeO. Igniting beryllium in air actually gives a mixture of BeO and the nitride Be3N2 together, but the direct oxide reaction itself is real and documented.
Strontium oxide or strontia, SrO, is formed when strontium reacts with oxygen — burning strontium in air gives a mixture with the nitride too, but the direct oxide route is real.
Barium oxide from metallic barium readily forms from its exothermic oxidation with dioxygen in air: 2 Ba(s) + O2(g) → 2 BaO(s).
When caesium burns in air, the superoxide CsO2 is the main product — the same overshoot potassium and rubidium show one row up, rather than a simple oxide.
Calcium hydride is prepared from its elements by direct combination of calcium and hydrogen at 300 to 400°C.
Mg + H2 → MgH2. First reported in 1951: direct hydrogenation of magnesium metal at high pressure and temperature (200 atmospheres, 500°C) with an MgI2 catalyst.
Strontium hydride can be prepared by combining strontium and hydrogen: Sr + H2 → SrH2, though a clean, near-quantitative yield needs oxygen-free conditions and redistilled strontium.
Barium hydride can be prepared by reacting elemental barium with hydrogen at relatively high temperatures, between 150 and 200°C.
2 Na + H2 → 2 NaH. Industrially, NaH is prepared by introducing molten sodium into mineral oil with hydrogen at atmospheric pressure, mixed vigorously.
Potassium hydride is produced by direct combination of the metal and hydrogen at temperatures between 200 and 350°C.
Rubidium hydride is synthesized by treating rubidium metal with hydrogen.
The documented route is indirect, not raw caesium metal meeting hydrogen gas: caesium hydride can be produced by heating caesium carbonate and metallic magnesium in hydrogen at 580 to 620°C.
Beryllium nitride is prepared by heating beryllium metal powder with dry nitrogen in an oxygen-free atmosphere at temperatures between 700 and 1,400°C: 3 Be + N2 → Be3N2.
It can be produced by direct reaction of the elements: 3 Ca + N2 → Ca3N2.
Strontium nitride, Sr3N2, is produced by burning strontium metal in air (resulting in a mixture with strontium oxide) or in nitrogen.

No dedicated article covers Ba3N2 the way it does for its neighbors, but barium's own element page confirms the reaction: reactions with other nonmetals, such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, silicon and hydrogen, proceed upon heating.

The compound can be obtained by absorption of N2 by metallic radium: 3 Ra + N2 → Ra3N2 — the black surface layer that forms on radium exposed to air is this nitride, not an oxide, since radium reacts with nitrogen before oxygen.
Br2 + 3 F2 → 2 BrF3, first described by Paul Lebeau in 1906 by reacting bromine with fluorine directly at 20°C.
First synthesized by Henri Moissan in 1891 by burning solid iodine in fluorine gas: I2 + 5 F2 → 2 IF5, still the method used today.

Interhalogen compounds like BrCl form by combining two pure halogens directly under the right conditions — the same family mechanism as chlorine trifluoride and iodine monochloride, just without a dedicated compound article of its own.
Iodine monochloride is produced simply by combining the halogens in a 1:1 molar ratio: I2 + Cl2 → 2 ICl, passing chlorine gas through iodine crystals.
Iodine monobromide is formed when iodine and bromine are combined directly: I2 + Br2 → 2 IBr.
Hydrogen bromide is produced by combining hydrogen and bromine at temperatures between 200 and 400°C, typically catalyzed by platinum.
H2 + I2 → 2 HI, a reaction that can be catalyzed by platinum and is used to generate high-purity samples.
A trade association coined the word chevon for it in 1922 — chevre crossed with mouton — and the USDA adopted it in 1928. Nobody used it. In South Asia the word for goat meat is simply mutton.
Nearly all male cattle are castrated as calves for beef or work. The minority left intact grow up into the bull that breeds the herd's next generation.
Female calves with the right breeding are raised up rather than sold — kept as replacement cows for the very herd their mothers belong to.
The female counterpart to a bull is a cow; a castrated male is a steer, ox or bullock — the choice of word tracks region and purpose more than biology.
Oxen are commonly castrated adult male cattle, trained to draught in a yoke — castration makes them calm enough to work in harness rather than fight it.
A heifer that finally calves earns the name cow — the replacement heifers a dairy herd holds back become the herd itself, one generation on.
Other than the few bulls kept for breeding, nearly all male cattle are castrated and slaughtered for meat before the age of three — a steer is exactly that animal, raised for beef rather than work.
Hens stay on the nest about two days after the first chick hatches, brooding the rest to keep them warm while the newly hatched feed on their last yolk.
Chick is simply the word for a young chicken of either sex; cockerel and pullet are what the two sexes are called once they are old enough to tell apart.
Pullets are raised on feed toward their first egg — sexually immature by definition, and under 22 weeks old in the poultry industry's own usage.
'Rooster' displaced 'cock' in North American usage from the 18th century on — probably to sidestep the word's other meaning, not because the bird changed.
A pullet stops being immature and starts laying in earnest — a hen bred for it can produce more than 300 eggs in a single year.
Caponising is done young, before the cockerel it targets ever becomes a rooster — a male chicken castrated or neutered, traditionally to make the meat milder and fattier.
The chicken card already lays eggs generically; a hen is the specific bird that actually does it — an adult female bred for laying can produce more than 300 a year.
Rams needed for breeding, or valuable enough for their genetics, are usually the only male sheep past puberty that are not castrated.
A ewe and her direct descendants often move as one unit within a larger flock — sheep relationships stay closest among related animals.
Lamb marking, ear tagging, docking and castrating are all carried out together, several weeks after birth. Most male lambs get the cut; a few rams do not.
Gestation runs about 150 days, and birthing — kidding — usually produces twins rather than a single kid alone.
Bucks of Swiss and northern breeds come into rut each autumn, when a strong, distinctive odour sets an intact male apart from a wether at ten paces.
Many breeders postpone breeding until a doe reaches 70% of her adult weight — though on open range that kind of separation from the herd is rarely possible.
A sow digs a body-sized hollow in the last day before farrowing and gives birth lying down, unlike most other hoofed animals, which give birth standing.
Most male piglets are castrated. The ones kept intact for breeding are simply given time to reach it — a boar is a male pig of breeding age, nothing more.
Feeder pigs sold on to be finished for slaughter are weaned gilts or barrows between 18 and 37 kg — a gilt simply a young female not yet mated or farrowed.
Barrow and stag name the same operation at two different ages: barrow is castrated before puberty, stag after. Nearly all male pigs not kept for breeding are cut young.
The word changes with the litter, not a birthday: a gilt becomes a sow once she has farrowed her first or second time, whichever local usage counts.
Most market hogs sold for slaughter are weaned gilts or barrows — a barrow, castrated before puberty, is one of the two animals pork most often actually comes from.
When the mare gives birth she is 'foaling', the birth itself usually stated as 'to foal', and what results, newborn, is 'foaled' — a foal until its first birthday.
After weaning from its dam a foal is called a weanling, then simply ages onward as colt or filly — the sex-specific names that hold until three or four.
Colt and filly are the same word twice over, split only by sex — both used from birth until the horse reaches three or four years old.
When young horses reach breeding maturity the terms change again: a colt over three years old — four, in horse racing — is a stallion from then on.
A filly over three years old — four in horse racing — is called a mare from then on; the same age line that turns a colt into a stallion.
A gelding is called that regardless of age — the only horse term that does not shift at puberty, because castration is what defines it, not the calendar.
When a mare gives birth she is 'foaling' — the more precise version of the same event the generic horse card already stands in for.
Swamp buffaloes wallow deliberately, digging mudholes with their horns and coating themselves in mud — water and mud both matter to how they keep cool.
In India and Nepal the same meat is called red beef or buff; in the Philippines, where the name was coined in the 1970s, it is carabeef.
The African wild ass lives in the deserts and arid country of the Horn of Africa — drier ground than the grassland that drew in the horse. Domesticated there some 5,000 to 7,000 years ago.
Rabbits live alone or in groups in nests or burrows dug into the ground, grazing the grass around them — livestock since Roman cuniculture, at the latest.
A duckling is a young duck in downy plumage — the word covers everything from newly hatched to a young adult still tender enough for the table.
A duckling grows into whichever adult name fits its sex — drake for the male, duck (or 'hen', in ornithology) for the female it already shares a name with.
A duckling raised up rather than sold on for the tender-meat trade simply becomes a duck — 'duck' already naming the adult female, 'hen' in ornithology.
Greylag geese, ancestor of most domestic geese, feed chiefly on grasses and are often found grazing in pastures alongside sheep or cows — needing water close by too.
Young geese are called goslings only up until they fledge — the point their flight feathers finish growing in and they can finally fly.
'Goose' alone can mean either sex, but set beside 'gander' it narrows to the female — the pairing is what does the work, not either word by itself.
A gosling that fledges into a female is simply a goose — the collective term for a group of them is a gaggle on the ground, a skein or a wedge in flight.
Geese are eaten too, same as the domestic fowl already on this table — cut for meat exactly the way chicken, duck and turkey already are.
Wild turkey hens lay a clutch of 10 to 14 eggs, incubated at least 28 days; what hatches out, precocial and already able to leave the nest within a day, is a poult.
An adult male turkey — tom or gobbler, either name works — normally weighs 5 to 11 kg, close to twice the 2.5 to 5.4 kg of the adult female.
The adult female turkey is typically much smaller than the male — 2.5 to 5.4 kg against the tom's 5 to 11 — though both come from the same poult.
Basking sharks are the second-largest fish alive, after the whale shark. Slow and harmless, they filter zooplankton by swimming open-mouthed along the cool, productive currents of temperate coasts.

A deep-sea filter feeder first caught in 1976 and still barely known — fewer than 300 have ever been recorded. It spends daylight hours in the near-freezing water below 150 m, rising each night to feed where it is warmer.

A placid, slow-moving shark of sandy shorelines and submerged reefs, despite a permanent mouthful of ragged, protruding teeth. Only one embryo per litter survives — it eats its smaller womb-mates before birth.

The ocean's best-known apex predator, patrolling temperate coastal currents and continental shelves. A blood-vessel network called the rete mirabile keeps its stomach several degrees warmer than the water around it.
The fastest shark known, reaching bursts of 74 km/h (46 mph) through open ocean currents. Prized as a game fish for its habit of leaping high into the air once hooked by anglers.
Named for its favourite prey — it turns up in large numbers during Alaskan salmon runs. Vascular heat exchangers let it hold its stomach 16-19°C above the near-freezing sub-Arctic Pacific around it.
The upper lobe of its tail can be as long as the rest of its body, and it is a weapon: threshers whip the water to stun schooling fish before turning back to feed on the catch.

A deep-sea shark of dark continental slopes and soft sea-floor sediment, its long electroreceptive snout finds prey by their electric field alone. Elastic jaw ligaments let it launch its jaws forward at up to 3.14 m/s to catch it.
A white-spotted ray of shallow coral reefs and bays, famous for leaping clear of the water. Its chevron-shaped teeth are built to crush the shells of the molluscs and crustaceans it feeds on.

The largest ray alive, with a wingspan up to 7 metres and the largest brain of any fish. It filter-feeds on zooplankton carried past coral-reef cleaning stations by the current, though most of its diet comes from deeper water.

A small, spotted bottom-dweller of muddy and sandy seafloors, no more than a metre long. Its eggs are laid in a horny, tendrilled case — a 'mermaid's purse' — anchored to the seabed until the pup hatches.

Also called the school shark, this slender predator ranges the temperate continental shelf worldwide. Tagging has tracked individuals travelling thousands of kilometres, from Britain as far as the Azores and Iceland.
A harmless, wary bottom-forager of muddy and sandy bay flats and kelp beds along the Pacific coast, more active at night than day. Only one human incident has ever been recorded, in 1955.
Nicknamed the 'garbage can of the sea' for the widest diet of any shark. Sea turtles are a genuine preference, not an accident — they turn up in as much as 20.8% of stomachs studied.
Pups shelter for their first years in shallow mangrove nurseries before moving out onto open sand flats as adults. The yellow-brown skin that gives it its name is camouflage over a sandy seabed.

One of the few sharks that can thrive in fresh water — tracked 4,000 km up the Amazon and resident in Lake Nicaragua. Territorial in the shallow, murky coastal waters it shares with people, it is one of three species most often implicated in bites.

The largest member of the dolphin family, not a whale at all. An apex predator with no natural predators of its own, it hunts fish, seals, sharks and even other whales, most densely in cold, high-latitude waters.

The last living member of a subclass otherwise gone for hundreds of millions of years. It lives on the deep slopes of coral reefs, regulating buoyancy in its chambered shell and reaching out with 50 to 90 tentacles.

A coastal shark of shallow bays, reef drop-offs and mangrove estuaries, easily told by the black edges on every fin. Feeding runs through schools of small fish often end in a spinning leap clear of the surface.

A wide-ranging open-ocean shark, historically blamed for attacks on shipwreck survivors — including sailors of the USS Indianapolis in 1945 — that earned it the name 'shipwreck shark'. Now critically endangered, down some 98% from overfishing.
Named for the smooth feel of its densely packed skin denticles. It shadows schools of tuna so reliably that, off Ghana, 'almost every tuna school has silky sharks trailing behind'.

Among the most abundant sharks on tropical coral reefs, from South Africa to the Pacific islands. It favours the shallowest reef flats and atoll lagoons, where its black-tipped dorsal fin often breaks the surface.

Groups of five to twenty gather by day near reef drop-offs and current-swept channels, splitting up at night to hunt alone. Cornered, it was the first shark species recorded performing a hunched threat display before attacking.

Unlike most requiem sharks, which must keep swimming to breathe, this reef-dweller can pump water over its gills and rest still in a coral cave by day. By night it hunts fish and octopus through reef crevices in packs.

The largest hammerhead, a solitary, nomadic predator ranging reefs, lagoons and continental shelves worldwide. Electroreceptors across its wide, hammer-shaped head detect the buried stingrays it specialises in hunting.

Famous for schooling hundreds strong near seamounts and offshore islands, unusually social for a hammerhead. Its scalloped, notched head lets it burrow into the seafloor and pin stingrays down. Critically endangered by overfishing.
An octopus has no shell and no internal skeleton either — the whole body, mantle and all eight arms, is muscle wrapped around itself, a design known as a muscular hydrostat.
The largest octopus species breeds only once: a female lays up to 100,000 eggs, guards them without eating for around six months, and dies as the last of them hatch.
The tetrodotoxin loaded into its bite is not made by the octopus itself — it comes from bacteria living inside its own salivary glands, the same broad family of toxin pufferfish also carry.
Every other cephalopod hunts. This one is a sedentary scavenger: it collects sinking detritus and dead plankton with a pair of retractile filaments instead of feeding tentacles.
Ink from a sac at the back of the mantle covers its retreat, and behind it sit the largest eyes of any living animal, up to 27 cm across, watching the dark for its one real predator, the sperm whale.

The shell is walled off into as many as 30 gas-filled chambers, and a living tube called the siphuncle runs through them, pumping salt to draw water out or in — buoyancy built on the same principle as a fish's swim bladder.

A scyphozoan polyp buds off a whole stack of young jellyfish at once. A cubozoan polyp does not: it was reclassified out of Scyphozoa in 1973 specifically because it lacks that step, and simply transforms in place into one medusa.

A scyphozoan polyp buds off young that drift away and grow into free-swimming jellyfish. Left to grow in cold water, one becomes the largest jellyfish alive — a bell over 2 m across trailing tentacles once measured past 36 m.

Every part of it — float, tentacles, feeding and reproductive structures — is a separate zooid budded from one fertilised egg and fused into a single colony, the same principle already at work in a coral head. The float itself is a gas-filled sac that works on the same buoyancy principle as a fish's swim bladder, just filled by the animal's own gas gland rather than swallowed air.

A sea anemone is essentially a single, oversized polyp — the same body plan as a coral polyp, just never covered over by a stony skeleton. Clownfish are not affected by their host anemone's sting and shelter among its tentacles in return.

Like every echinoderm it builds a skeleton of calcium-carbonate plates just under the skin rather than a shell around it — and it wears that skeleton onto a reef, grazing living coral polyps down to bare rock.

The largest fish alive, and one of the few sharks that feeds directly on clouds of eggs released during mass coral and fish spawning — a reliable enough food source that whale sharks gather predictably at reef sites like Ningaloo Reef to eat it.

Lays a large egg capsule fringed with hair-like fibres that anchor it to the reef substrate until the pup hatches. Adults hunt for molluscs and crustaceans by working their narrow snouts into reef crevices.

A nocturnal bottom-dweller of muddy and sandy coastal flats, motionless enough by day that it forms sedentary daytime groups. It is an obligate suction feeder, generating some of the strongest suction forces measured in any fish to pull prey from the seafloor.
In the total darkness of the deep sea, it dangles a modified fin ray — the illicium, tipped with a light-producing lure called the esca — to draw curious fish close enough to strike.
A bathydemersal 'sea toad' that rests on both soft sand and hard rocky substrate across the continental shelf, at depths between 200 and 1,000 metres.
First photographed alive by recreational divers exploring reefs near Ambon Island, Indonesia, in January 2008 — a species new to science, described the following year.
An ambush predator that lurks in reef caves and wrecks before lunging at whatever passes — fish, crustaceans, small sharks and rays, and juvenile sea turtles, all swallowed whole.
Camouflaged so well as an encrusted lump of reef rock that swimmers step on it by accident — and it is the most venomous fish known, with dorsal spines that can deliver a fatal sting.

Native to the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean's coral reefs, it was first recorded in the Mediterranean off Israel in 1991 after entering through the human-built Suez Canal, armed with 13 long, venomous dorsal spines that have caused human deaths.

A cat-sized carnivore, proportioned like a civet and at least partly a tree-climber, ranging the treed valleys and flatlands of Eurasia. Most studies place it as the basal member of the whole cat family, and a likely ancestor of Pseudaelurus.

Grew from cat-sized to about 5 feet as the animals it hunted grew bigger, spreading through Europe, Asia and North America over the Miocene. Fossils show it shared its bone structure with modern cats, and it is considered ancestral to essentially every cat alive today.

A genuine side branch, not a step toward the tiger: Machairodontinae, the sabertooth-cat subfamily, is the earliest-diverging branch of the whole cat family and DNA shows it isn't closely related to any living cat. Homotherium ranged across Eurasia, Africa and North America — a mummified cub recovered from Siberian permafrost still had its wide, rounded paws built for snow.

The lineage that led to today's big cats: Pantherinae split from the rest of the cat family in the Miocene. Panthera zdanskyi's skull, unearthed in Gansu, China and dated to about 2.5 million years ago, is the oldest complete pantherine skull ever found — its describers named it the 'Longdan tiger' for how closely it resembles a modern tiger's, though later studies argue it may be the same species as the slightly older Panthera palaeosinensis.

The modern tiger, Panthera tigris. The earliest fossils attributed to the species itself are jaw fragments from Lantian, China, dated to the early Pleistocene — not long after Panthera zdanskyi's own skull, the closest fossil match yet found to how the tiger's distinctive look began.

Not an ancestor of the modern tiger, but a subspecies of it: tigers colonised the Sunda Islands over a land bridge during the last glacial period, and rising seas then isolated Java's population from the mainland's. Since a 2017 revision it's classified as the same subspecies as the Sumatran and Bali tigers, P. t. sondaica. The last confirmed sighting was in 1976; it was declared extinct in 2008.

Pakicetus was a wolf-like mammal that foraged along Pakistan's rivers about 50 million years ago, wading in for fish. It's the earliest recognized cetacean, identified not by its legs but by a dense, air-filled inner-ear bone every whale still has.

Within a few million years the pakicetid line produced fully amphibious hunters like Ambulocetus — crocodile-like, with a long snout and eyes on top of its skull for hunting half-submerged, but hind legs still powerful enough to bear its weight on land.

The protocetids that followed, like Rodhocetus, swam mainly by paddling with their hind feet rather than walking. Their sacrum lost the fused vertebrae that anchor a leg to a spine for weight-bearing, so on land they could only shuffle on their bellies.

By the time of Basilosaurus, the hind limbs had shrunk to a pair of legs just 35 cm long in some specimens — too small to ever reach the ground, and likely kept only for grasping during mating. It never returned to land again.

Basilosaurus and Dorudon shared late Eocene seas — and the same food chain: fossilized Basilosaurus stomachs held young Dorudon bones. Dorudon's build carries forward — short spine, true tail fluke, swum by oscillating up and down like every living whale.

Within that dorudontine lineage the skull lengthened and the teeth simplified into worn, gapped pegs. Llanocetus, an early mysticete, still gripped and sheared prey with those teeth — baleen hadn't evolved yet, but the broad mysticete jaw already had.

Stem mysticetes like Llanocetus fed by gripping and suction rather than filtering. Later members of the same lineage lost their teeth for good, replacing them with baleen — keratin filter plates that let a modern baleen whale strain krill from open water by the ton.

Dogs did not descend from any wolf alive today. DNA shows all dogs and wolves share a common ancestor: a Late Pleistocene wolf population, now extinct, whose lineage split from today's wolves somewhere between 27,000 and 40,000 years ago — long before there was any farming for a dog to be useful to.

Bred for many generations in China purely as a companion, with no working job at all — pet pugs were valued highly enough by Chinese emperors that the royal dogs were kept in luxury and guarded by soldiers. Dutch traders carried the breed to Europe in the 16th century, where it became a favourite of European royalty, Queen Victoria among them.

Developed by the Chukchi people of the Chukchi Peninsula in eastern Siberia as a sled-pulling and companion dog able to survive extreme cold, with a double coat built to withstand temperatures as low as -50 to -60°C. Introduced to Alaska around 1908 during the Nome Gold Rush, it went on to dominate sled-dog racing on a combination of speed and endurance.

Bred in the hill country of the England-Scotland border to herd sheep using 'the eye' — a fixed, intimidating stare that moves a flock without the dog touching it. Stanley Coren's 1994 survey of obedience-trial judges ranked it the most trainable of 138 breeds tested, and it is often called the most intelligent dog breed.

Max von Stephanitz founded the breed in 1899 from traditional German herding dogs that worked sheep and cattle across the pasture, breeding strictly for intelligence and working ability rather than looks. That same working drive later made the breed a mainstay of police, military, search-and-rescue and disability-assistance work.

The breed descends from Roman legion drover dogs that helped move cattle over the Alps to feed the army. Those dogs interbred with local dogs around the German town of Rottweil, where butchers used them to herd cattle and other livestock and pull carts of meat to market — earning the breed its old name, the 'Rottweil butcher's dog.'

Monks at the Great St Bernard Hospice, on a treacherous Alpine pass between Switzerland and Italy, began keeping dogs around 1660 and by the mid-1700s were using them for search and rescue — strong enough to cross deep snow drifts and track lost travelers by scent. One dog, Barry, is credited with saving somewhere between 40 and 100 lives.

Basenjis come from the old-growth forest of the Congo Basin in Central Africa, where villagers used them to drive game silently through the wood and into nets. Its unusually shaped larynx cannot produce a true bark — instead it makes a yodel-like sound, which is how it earned the name 'the barkless dog.'

Historically used for hunting in the open, where its pursuit speed and keen eyesight — rather than scent — let it chase down prey across open fields by sight, a technique called coursing. Its light, muscular build, large heart and flexible spine let it reach peak speeds of at least 69 km/h (43 mph).

One of the oldest dog lineages, genetically distinct from most breeds first developed in the 19th century. Its thick, fine, silky coat evolved as protection from the harsh mountain climate of Afghanistan, and its large paw pads act as shock absorbers on rocky ground.

Descended from hounds bred by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert in Belgium to hunt deer and wild boar by scent — bred so carefully that they were known as 'blooded hounds,' hounds of pure lineage, likely the origin of the name. Its olfactory bulb is roughly 40 times bigger than a human's relative to brain size, letting it follow a trail days old; canine identification like this has been accepted as evidence in some courts.

Bred primarily for hunting rabbit and hare by scent, a pursuit known as beagling. Its keen nose and unintimidating size later made it the breed of choice for the US Department of Agriculture's 'Beagle Brigade,' which sniffs airport luggage for prohibited food.

The name comes from German Dachs (badger) and Hund (dog): the breed was built to scent, chase, and dig badgers and other burrowing animals out of the soil. Its short legs and long body suit tunnel work, its oversized front paws are shaped like paddles for digging, and its loose skin keeps from tearing underground.

Developed by the Reverend John 'Jack' Russell starting in 1819 from a terrier named Trump, purpose-built to run alongside mounted foxhound packs across the meadows and countryside of North Devon, then go to ground and bolt the fox from its den once the hounds ran it there.

Descends from 'bull and terrier' dogs bred for bull-baiting, in which a bull was tethered by a collar and rope staked to the ground while dogs attacked it. After the sport was outlawed, James Hinks crossed these fighting dogs with the English White Terrier in the 1850s-60s to breed a cleaner-looking dog, fixing the breed's now-famous egg-shaped head by 1862.

Descended from St. John's water dogs bred by fishermen in Newfoundland to haul nets and retrieve fish from the water, brought to Britain in the 1830s and crossed with British hunting dogs. Its 'soft mouth' — the ability to carry game and waterfowl without damaging it — made it the standard retriever, and by 2006 the UK and US each had more than twice as many registered Labradors as the next most popular breed.

Bred at the Guisachan estate in the Scottish Highlands beginning in the 1860s by Dudley Marjoribanks, Lord Tweedmouth, who crossed a Flat-coated Retriever with a Tweed Water Spaniel — later adding Red Setter, Labrador and Bloodhound blood — to build a gundog able to retrieve shot ducks and other game from both water and land.

Named for the Mexican state of Chihuahua, most of which lies in the Chihuahuan Desert, where Spanish conquistadors found small dogs already plentiful. The modern breed is the smallest recognized in the world, with an ideal weight of just 1.5 to 2.5 kg (3.3 to 5.5 lb).
A demersal fish of the cold North Atlantic that hunts and rests along the seafloor, favouring coarse bottom sediment — gravel, rock and shell — over mud or fine sand.
A small schooling fish of the open sea that filters zooplankton from the water — copepods, mysids and krill, all shrimp-like crustaceans — in schools that can hold billions of individuals.
A cold-water fish of clear rivers and streams; some populations, called steelhead, migrate out to the ocean and back to spawn several times over their lives rather than dying after a single run.

An ambush predator that lies hidden and motionless in the weedy, muddy margins of northern rivers and lakes until prey — often a smaller fish, sometimes a smaller pike — strays within striking range, then attacks in a fraction of a second.

A hardy bottom-feeding fish tolerant of water too muddy and low in oxygen for most other fish, foraging through the mud for insect larvae, small crustaceans and other invertebrates; Roman fish-farmers were already raising it in ponds two thousand years ago.

Bred from colour-mutated wild carp in Chinese ponds for over a thousand years; Ming-dynasty breeders moved them into ceramic pots indoors, where mutations that couldn't have survived an open pond could finally be spotted and bred on.

An ornamental variety of Amur carp, originally raised as a food fish in the rice paddies of Niigata, Japan; farmers there began breeding for colour mutations in the 1820s, eventually developing the fancy varieties known as nishikigoi.
Lives the reverse of a salmon's life: it grows for years in European rivers, then swims back down current, thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea in the mid-Atlantic, to spawn once and die.
Europe's largest native freshwater fish, scaleless and covered in slime, it lies along the muddy riverbed using six barbels to smell and feel for annelid worms, snails, insects and other fish.

Loses every tooth and scale by adulthood, hunting instead with a flattened bill; special organs beside its eyes and brain burn energy purely to keep its vision 10 to 15°C warmer than the cold water hundreds of metres down where it hunts.

One of the largest and fastest bony fish in the open sea, reaching 5 metres and over 800 kilograms; it flares rows of blue and lavender stripes down its flanks in a coordinated flash just before striking a school of prey.

Hatches from a drifting egg looking like any ordinary fish, symmetrical with an eye on each side; within weeks one eye migrates across its skull to sit beside the other, and it settles flat onto the sandy seabed, camouflaged on its blind side.

The male, not the female, gets pregnant: she deposits her eggs into his brood pouch, and he carries, nourishes and oxygenates them for up to 45 days before giving birth — anchoring his prehensile tail to kelp and seagrass in between to avoid being swept away.

Lives nestled in the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone on the reef, protected by a mucus coating that mimics the anemone's own chemistry so it isn't stung — in return it drives off anemone-eating fish and fans in oxygenated water.

A freshwater fish of South American rivers whose pack-hunter reputation is a myth — most species are omnivores that school mainly for protection. The bite is genuinely strong: crowded Brazilian swimming spots have seen dozens bitten on the feet at once.

The male alone builds a nest scooped into gravel in sunlit shallows, then guards the eggs and newly hatched fry for weeks against anything that comes close — a level of parental care that has helped it spread as an invasive species from Japan to Guatemala.

Introduced to Lake Victoria in the 1950s, this apex predator ate through the lake's native cichlids so completely that it now survives mainly on shrimp and minnows — one of history's most damaging invasive species, blamed for several hundred fish extinctions.

The small white, or 'cabbage white', lays its eggs singly on cabbage and other brassica leaves. The caterpillars that hatch feed on the leaves through five instars before pupating into an adult butterfly.
A mated queen ant starts a colony by laying and tending eggs in an underground nest dug into the soil. The sterile female workers that hatch from those eggs go on to run every part of the colony.
Overwintering ladybirds gather in large clusters, sheltering under tree bark and boulders or amid leaf litter and dead vegetation, before waking in spring to hunt aphids.
A dung beetle larva feeds on the dung around it, and tunnelling species such as Euoniticellus intermedius dig burrows into the soil to bury a ball of dung there for storage.

Firefly larvae overwinter by burrowing into soil or sheltering on or under tree bark, before an adult's glow — a chemical reaction between the enzyme luciferase and the compound luciferin — signals for a mate in the dark.

A dragonfly spends most of its life underwater as a nymph, up to five years in large species, preying on other invertebrates and even small fish before finally emerging into the air as a winged adult.

A locust is a grasshopper that feeds on grasses and crops; at high population density it shifts into a swarming, gregarious phase and takes to the air, flying with the prevailing wind for up to 150 km in a single day.

A praying mantis's body is cryptically coloured to blend into leaves and grass, and it waits motionless there for prey — raptorial forelegs lined with spines snap shut in a single strike once something wanders close.
A cockroach hides by day in narrow crevices, tucked under a stone or among dead leaves, and emerges at night to scavenge on almost any organic matter, a compost heap included.
